name: Chitosan
lead: Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide made by partially deacetylating chitin, which is found mainly in the shells of shrimp and crabs and in some fungi and insects [1][2]. It dissolves in dilute acid and is widely used in medicine, agriculture and industry, with cosmetic uses and weight-loss supplements being the applications most relevant to appearance [1][2].

In appearance contexts it appears in two main forms: as a carrier polymer in topical and nanoparticle formulations, for example to improve skin retention of actives such as resveratrol [3][4], and as an over-the-counter 'fat binder' supplement. Wikipedia reports that reviews in 2008 and 2016 found no significant effect of chitosan on weight or cholesterol, and that the US FDA issued a 2015 advisory about exaggerated weight-loss claims by supplement retailers [1]. Sources reviewed contain no controlled evidence that chitosan inhibits skin pigmentation in people.

paras: Chitosan consists of randomly distributed glucosamine and N-acetylglucosamine units; the degree of deacetylation commonly ranges from 60 to 100 percent [1][2]. Its amine groups become positively charged in acid, which underlies its film-forming, mucoadhesive and antimicrobial behaviour [2][5][6].

Charles Hatchett obtained what is now called chitin from crustacean shells in 1799, Charles Rouget produced a soluble deacetylated form in 1859, and Felix Hoppe-Seyler named it chitosan in 1894 [1]. Interest revived in the 1970s, and chitosan was first registered as an active ingredient for sale in 1986 [1].

Chitosan is widely studied as a vehicle for delivering drugs and cosmetic actives through hydrogels, nanoparticles and emulsions [7][8][9]. In a laboratory study with porcine skin, chitosan/gum Arabic Pickering emulsions raised retention of resveratrol and improved its photostability [3].
Chitosan is used in haemostatic dressings and wound dressings [1][10][11]. A 2010 review reported antimicrobial properties [12].
Chitosan is sold as a fat binder. Wikipedia cites reviews finding no significant effect on weight or cholesterol, and a 2015 FDA advisory on exaggerated claims [1].

Grokipedia notes that chitosan from crustacean sources can carry allergenic proteins and variable purity [2]. The FDA classification of chitosan as generally recognised as safe is reported in the same source [2].

No studies found examining chitosan for skin pigmentation or other cosmetic appearance outcomes. Registered trials concern dental, haemostatic and other medical uses, for example chitosan powder in a cervical excision procedure [13] and chitosan mouthwash for dental black stains in children [14]. Reviews cited by Wikipedia found no significant weight-loss effect of chitosan supplements [1].

card.summary: A shellfish-derived polysaccharide used as a carrier in cosmetics and sold as a fat binder, with no trial showing a skin-pigment or appearance effect.
card.note: Crustacean-derived forms may carry allergenic proteins; weight-loss reviews report no significant effect.

quick.overview:
Chitosan is a natural polymer made from chitin in shellfish shells. For appearance it mainly shows up as a delivery carrier in skincare formulations and as a weight-loss supplement.

I found no human studies of chitosan for skin pigmentation. Reviews cited by Wikipedia report no significant weight or cholesterol effect from supplements.
quick.mechanism: Its amine groups become positively charged in acid, letting it form films, gels and nanoparticles that stick to tissue and carry other ingredients.
quick.risks: Crustacean-derived chitosan may carry allergenic proteins, according to Grokipedia. The FDA warned in 2015 about exaggerated weight-loss claims.
